To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we did not find any associations between genetic variants and survival in breast cancer patients who were treated with cyclophosphamidewith or without adjuvant chemotherapy or tamoxifen.

we found a lower risk of developing severe hematologic toxicity with cyclophosphomide among women with variant glutathione S-transferase P1 (GSTP1) alleles and that we did not find an association between any of the other genetic variants in our study and disease free survival in women treated with cyclophosmamide-containing chemotherapy.
known functional polymorphisms of genes involved in CP metabolism are not associated with DFS in breast cancer but are associated with a lower risk of developing severe neutropenia and leucopenias.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of genetic biomarkers to identify women at increased risk of developing adverse effects from chemotherapy and to identify women who are at increased risk of recurrence after chemotherapy.
the identification of biomarkers of treatment toxicity and response.
the identification and characterization of genetic polymorphisms that may be used to identify individuals who are at increased risk of toxicity and/or who will benefit from a specific treatment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence to support the routine use of pharmacogenetic testing in the management of breast cancer.
genetic markers for CP metabolism do not have a major impact on outcomes in breast cancer, but may be useful in predicting toxicity.
the results of this study do not support the use of genetic markers in the clinical setting to predict outcomes in patients treated with CP-containing adjuvant therapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the genetic variants studied here do not appear to be useful for predicting DFS in patients treated with CP-based adjuvant therapy, but may have some utility in predicting toxicity in the subset of women treated with CP.

we found no evidence that genetic polymorphisms in CP metabolism pathway genes were associated with DFS, but that women who carried the GSTP1 G variant allele had a lower risk of grade 4 and 5 neutropenia and leucopenias.

the known functional genetic polymorphisms in genes involved in the metabolism of cyclophosphamides do not appear to have major effects on survival in breast cancer patients, although women who have a variant in GSTP1 may be less likely to develop grade 3 or 4 neutropenic toxicity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
genetic variants in genes in CP pharmacogenetics pathway are unlikely to have a major effect on disease-free survival in breast cancer patients treated with CP.

genetic variants in the genes involved in cyclophosphamidemetabolism pathway are not predictive of disease-free survival in breast cancer patients who received cyclophosphamine-containing chemotherapy.
genetic variants in genes that encode for enzymes involved in CP pharmacology are not predictive of DFS in breast cancer.
